clips.text: You step off the kerb — and your shoe stays dry.
clips.image: ACTION/AFTERMATH: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie stepping off a rainy city kerb, one shoe hovering over a puddle, the shoe completely dry, rain falling, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, cinematic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: hook sentence 1 ONLY (~4s); ACTION/AFTERMATH image (mid-step, shoe dry, rain visible); aggressive zoom-punch; 350ms pause after a1 (GAP); bed in after this sentence. MODERN-DISCOMFORT COLD OPEN: the expected cold soak is the ground, the dry shoe is the break.

clips.text: Thirty metres a second. That is how fast your foot has to hit the water — or you sink.
clips.image: PAYOFF FLASH (fresh image, NOT a crop): extreme close-up of a dry shoe striking a rain puddle, water exploding sideways in a frozen crown of droplets, the shoe still dry, rain visible, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, dramatic, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: payoff flash lands ~5s (a genuinely DIFFERENT dramatic image from a1). Key number 30 m/s spoken here; number visualised at c2 overlay + f2 recap — no pop here.

clips.text: Next: the slap, the stroke, the Moon — and one pause that sinks you.
clips.image: One frame with three zones: a foot slapping a puddle, a laboratory water tank, a grey Moon over a city rooftop, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, no text
clips.note: AUTOPSY: re-orientation TIGHT — 14 words, ~5s spoken (<= ~8s); music fades in ONLY after a1’s first spoken sentence.

clips.text: You know this feeling. Rain all morning. A puddle stretched across the kerb. You step in — and brace for the cold soak, the wet sock. Only this time, the cold never comes.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie bracing with a wince as he steps toward a wide rain puddle on a city kerb, rain falling, one foot raised, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: open loop 1 (mini): discomfort ground — the cold soak the viewer knows; tease overlay + push-in.

clips.text: Another step. Still dry. The puddle ripples under your shoe and closes again, like a door shutting. A bus hisses past. Nobody looks up. In a city of wet shoes, yours are the only dry pair.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie walking across a rain puddle on dry shoes, ripples closing behind each step, a bus hissing past in the background, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: escalation: the crossing widens.

clips.text: Here is the problem, plainly. Water does not hold people up. You weigh about seventy kilograms, and every step should punch through to the asphalt. So why are you still standing?
clips.image: A bathroom scale on wet asphalt beside a rain puddle, a man’s shadow stretching across the water, rain falling, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: key number 70 kg — overlay carries it; no pop.

clips.text: Because you are not standing on the water. You are beating it — one slap at a time, faster than eyes can follow. Slow one heartbeat, and the water remembers you. That is the first run.
clips.image: Close-up of a shoe slapping a puddle so fast the water blurs, droplets frozen mid-air, a second foot already lifting clear, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 2: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser.

clips.text: Chapter two: the first run. Forget walking. Nobody walks on water. You are sprinting on a surface trying to swallow your feet — winning by a fraction of a second, every step.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie sprinting across a wide rain-flooded street, feet skimming the water surface, rain falling, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, cinematic wide shot, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: First: the slap. Your foot comes down hard, punching a pocket of air into the water — a cavity, a hollow under your sole that lasts a blink. That pocket is your floor.
clips.image: Extreme slow-motion close-up of a shoe punching a hollow air pocket into a puddle, the cavity opening under the sole, water walls rising around it, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 15: the cavity visualised as a hollow under the sole.

clips.text: Second: the stroke. Before the pocket collapses, your foot pushes back, shoving the water down and sideways. The water pushes back — that is the lift. Most of your lift comes from this moment.
clips.image: Close-up of a foot pushing back against a collapsing air pocket in a puddle, water shoved down and sideways in a spray, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 15: the stroke visualised as water shoved down and sideways.

clips.text: Third: the recovery. You yank your foot out before the pocket caves in, before the water grabs your ankle. Too slow, and the cavity closes like a mouth. Too fast, and you never pushed. Three moves, under a second.
clips.image: Close-up of a foot yanking upward out of a puddle just as the air pocket caves shut behind it, droplets flying, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 15: the recovery visualised as the pocket snapping shut.

clips.text: Here is what it is not: surface tension. A water strider stands on surface tension because it weighs almost nothing. At your size, it holds up nothing. What holds you up is force: slap hard enough, fast enough, forever.
clips.image: A tiny water strider insect standing on the skin of a still puddle, beside it a human shoe sinking straight through the surface, rain falling, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: differentiator stated plainly: NOT surface tension at human scale; striders keep their physics.

clips.text: That word — forever — is the catch. A floor lasting a tenth of a second only works if the next step lands. No pausing to admire the view. No stopping to tie your shoe. The water takes its floor back.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie running across puddles, glancing down at his untied shoelace but unable to stop, rain falling, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: the never-stop price, stated plainly.

clips.text: So how fast is fast enough? The answer comes from a lizard, a lab, and a 1996 calculation — and the number is worse than you think. That is the lab.
clips.image: A speedometer needle buried at the top of its dial, rain droplets on the glass, a blurred runner reflected behind it, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 3: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser.

clips.text: Chapter three: the lab. The teacher is a green lizard from Central America — the basilisk — sprinting across rivers on its back legs. Its nickname, the Jesus Christ lizard, comes from the trick alone. The physics matters.
clips.image: A green basilisk lizard sprinting upright on its back legs across a river, feet slapping the surface, river green water, storm-grey sky, slate grey rain clouds, rain silver light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card. Religious-resonance guard: nickname mentioned ONCE, neutrally, physics-first. River green ONLY in this chapter (c1/c5/c7).

clips.text: In 1996, Glasheen and McMahon modelled the basilisk’s run and asked what a human would need. Their answer, published in Nature: about thirty metres a second — the foot moving DOWN, not forward — on every step.
clips.image: A 1990s science laboratory, a researcher in a white coat studying a water tank where a lizard runs across the surface, hand-drawn diagrams pinned on the wall, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, rain silver window light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: key number 30 m/s — overlay carries it; spoken as “about”; downward-vs-forward boundary explicit; impact SFX; no pop (overlay carries the number).

clips.text: And the power? About fifteen times more muscle power than a human body can produce. Fifteen of you, packed into one body — barely staying up. One classic calculation, remember. Other models give different numbers. None that a human can reach.
clips.image: Fifteen identical silhouettes of a running man stacked side by side, merging into one figure sprinting across a puddle, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: key number 15x — overlay carries it; “one classic calculation” boundary explicit; no pop.

clips.text: Slow the slap to ten metres a second, and a calculation by Bush and Hu demands something else: feet. Each foot would need about one square metre — a dinner table strapped to each ankle. Smaller feet, faster slap. Bigger feet, slower slap. No comfortable version.
clips.image: ONE lab asset, full view: a laboratory bench with a human shoe beside a dinner-table-sized flat foot panel, a small lizard model and a water tank arranged left to right, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 4: staged reveal, one asset; c5-c7 are true crops of this; Bush & Hu foot-size comparison.

clips.text: Now the lizard that can do it. A basilisk weighs about ninety grams — less than your phone. About eight strides a second, each foot slapping, stroking, lifting clear before the water closes. Ninety grams, eight strides a second, a lifetime of practice.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 lab asset, zoomed into the lizard zone: a small green basilisk lizard on a river-green water tank surface, a mobile phone beside it for scale, river green water, slate grey lab bench, rain silver light, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of c4 asset; 90 g / 8 Hz — never “20 steps/sec”; river green.

clips.text: In 2004, Hsieh and Lauder filmed the run in three dimensions, measuring the forces. Their finding, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences: most support comes from the slap itself — the first punch, not the push. Miss the slap, and nothing saves you.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 lab asset, zoomed into the force zone: a foot striking a water tank surface with arrows of motion bursting outward, a high-speed camera beside the tank, slate grey lab, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of c4 asset; Hsieh & Lauder 2004, slap finding.

clips.text: Fourth: the twist. The basilisk is not walking. It is sprinting — and it sinks the moment it slows. Adults cross a few metres; smaller ones go farther. No fixed distance. No finish line. Only speed, and the second you lose it.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the c4 lab asset, zoomed into the whole-bench zone: the basilisk lizard sprinting across river-green water, slowing and sinking at the far edge, river green water, storm-grey sky, slate grey clouds, rain silver light, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 4 = TWIST; true crop of c4 asset; crossing distance varies — no fixed distance as fact; river green.

clips.text: So the lab says no. The lizard says almost. And one more animal — far heavier — runs on water every spring. That is the grebe. And after it, the Moon.
clips.image: A grey dawn lake with two birds rushing across the surface in the distance, a full Moon fading in the morning sky above a rainy city skyline, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 4: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser.

clips.text: Chapter four: the heavier bird, and the Moon. If ninety grams feels like cheating, meet an animal sixteen times heavier that still runs on water.
clips.image: A western grebe standing on a grey dawn lake beside a tiny basilisk lizard on a floating leaf, the size difference stark, mist over the water, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: The western grebe weighs about one and a half kilograms. Every spring, two grebes rush across a lake side by side, wings spread, feet hammering the surface — a courtship dance called rushing. About twenty metres, crossed on foot.
clips.image: ONE grebe asset, full view: two western grebes rushing side by side across a grey dawn lake, wings spread wide, feet hammering the surface, spray flying, mist, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 1 of 3: staged reveal, one grebe asset; d3-d4 are true crops of this; 1.5 kg / 20 m.

clips.text: Seven strides a second, wings beating for lift, feet slapping too fast to see. The grebe is not defying the maths. It pays the price the maths demands: enormous effort, for a few seconds, for twenty metres — then it stops, and floats.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 grebe asset, zoomed into the feet zone: grebe feet hammering the lake surface in a blur of spray, wings beating above, grey dawn light, slate grey, rain silver, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 2: true crop of d2 asset; 7 Hz grebe stride.

clips.text: So the scale climbs: ninety grams, one and a half kilograms — then you, at seventy. Each step up costs power, speed, effort. The grebe proves the middle is possible — and the top brutal.
clips.image: TRUE CROP of the d2 grebe asset, zoomed into the whole-lake zone: the two grebes small against a vast grey lake, a human silhouette watching from the shore, mist, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, no text
clips.note: dataScene beat 3: true crop of d2 asset; scale comparison 90 g to 1.5 kg to 70 kg.

clips.text: Which brings us to the experiment nobody believed. In 2012, a team led by Minetti asked the question backwards: if gravity is the problem, what happens when it gets weaker? They built a rig to find out.
clips.image: A science laboratory in 2012, a wading pool with an empty harness hanging above it, small rigid fins laid out on the poolside, a researcher checking straps, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, rain silver window light, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: Minetti 2012 setup.

clips.text: Here is the rig. Volunteers ran in place in a wading pool, a harness taking most of their weight, small rigid fins on their feet — each under a tenth of a square metre. Nobody ran across a lake. Nobody went to the Moon. A lab, a harness, a pool.
clips.image: A volunteer in a harness running in place in a wading pool, small rigid fins strapped to the feet, water spraying, a researcher holding the harness frame, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty boundary explicit: harness + fins, running in place, nobody went to the Moon.

clips.text: And it worked — but only when gravity fell to about twenty-two percent of Earth’s. Near the Moon’s gravity, no higher. Above that line, they sank. Below it, they stayed up, running in place. The loophole is real. It is also useless.
clips.image: A large gravity dial in a laboratory turned down to near the bottom of its scale, a runner in a harness visible through the lab window behind it, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: key number 22% — overlay carries it; impact SFX; no pop.

clips.text: Useless, because the Moon has no open liquid water. No puddles, no lakes, no rivers — vacuum boils water away or freezes it solid. The one place the maths lets you run on water has no water to run on.
clips.image: The grey cratered surface of the Moon in a storm-grey palette, dry cracked ground, no water anywhere, Earth small in the black sky above, slate grey, rain silver earthlight, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: twist: no open liquid water on the Moon.

clips.text: So Earth says you cannot stop. The Moon says you cannot start. What is left is the test: one run, one pause, and whether you would keep this power. That is the test.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie standing at a riverbank at dawn, one foot raised over the water, deciding whether to run, mist over the river, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 5: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser.

clips.text: Chapter five: the test. You have heard the kerb, the run, the lab, and the Moon. Now the choice — and the pause — is yours.
clips.image: An empty riverbank at dawn, a pair of dry shoes placed neatly at the water’s edge, mist over the river, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Here is the test, from the real water-runners: run across the river at dawn, bank to bank, without stopping. Not for a photograph. Not for breath. Not to wave at the bridge. One pause, and the river takes you.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie sprinting across a wide river at dawn, people watching from a bridge above, never slowing, mist, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: the test, stated as the real water-runners’ rule.

clips.text: But here is the catch. Your muscles do not wait for permission. About fifteen times the power your body can make, in every step, at a foot speed no human leg has reached — you would burn your fuel in seconds. Your body would give out first.
clips.image: Close-up of a runner’s legs mid-stride on water, muscles straining, spray flying, the runner’s face tight with effort, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: muscle-fuel limit; no invented human stride frequency.

clips.text: And a second catch: you are not walking. You are sprinting, forever, on a floor vanishing under each foot. No standing on the water. No strolling across the lake. No pausing mid-river to watch the light. The power is never, ever stopping.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie sprinting across a lake, never pausing, never looking at the light on the water, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: second catch: sprinting forever, never strolling.

clips.text: So here is the question the story turns on: would you trade solid ground — the right to stand still — for the power to run across any water on Earth, as long as you never paused?
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie alone on a riverbank, looking down at the water, thinking, rain beginning to fall, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: RHETORICAL-QUESTION beat: rhetorical beat — slow drift + duck; 1.75s full silence after (GAP).

clips.text: There is no right answer. Only the answer your legs give — written the first time your lungs burned. Which brings us to today. That is the choice.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie walking away from the river toward a rainy city street, shoulders relaxed, decision made, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter-end open loop 6: tease overlay + push-in + 1s riser.

clips.text: One last thing about the test: pass it, and thank a ninety-gram lizard, a courting grebe, and three teams who measured the impossible. Fail it, and you are in the majority — every human who ever lived is on your side.
clips.image: A tiny basilisk lizard on a wet stone beside a grebe feather and a scientist’s notebook, rain falling, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text

clips.text: Chapter six: today. You still step off the kerb in the rain, still brace for the cold soak, still feel the water flood your shoe. Nothing has changed — except you know now what staying dry would take.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie stepping off a rainy city kerb into a puddle, water flooding over his shoe, bracing for the cold, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: chapter card

clips.text: Remember the numbers: about thirty metres a second, downward, every step; about fifteen times the power your body can make; eight strides a second for the lizard; twenty-two percent gravity for the loophole. One puddle, and physics in your way.
clips.image: Four glowing shapes floating over a rainy city street: a speeding foot, a stack of figures, a sprinting lizard, a small Moon, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, scientific illustration style, no text
clips.note: rule 15: numbers visualised; key numbers recap — overlay carries them; no pop.

clips.text: And remember the twist: the enemy was never the water. It was the pause. The water never said no. It said: as fast as you can, as long as you can, not one heartbeat slower. The basilisk takes that bargain. The grebe too. You decide.
clips.image: A single foot paused flat above a puddle, the water below it calm and waiting, rain falling around it, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: twist restated: the pause is the enemy.

clips.text: If you could run on water but never stop — not for one second — where is the first place you would run to? Tell us why.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie looking straight at camera in the rain, dry shoes, puddles reflecting neon around him, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: COMMENT QUESTION (locked, verbatim): 1.5s VO pause + deeper bed duck after (GAP).

clips.text: Science note, plainly: thirty metres a second and fifteen times the power are one classic model’s 1996 estimates, not a measured human attempt — other models give different numbers; the basilisk stride is eight per second, not twenty; Minetti’s result came from a harness and fins, running in place; surface tension really does hold up water striders — negligible only at human size.
clips.image: Calm rainy city panorama, puddles reflecting neon, one figure walking with an umbrella in the distance, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: uncertainty recap, explicit.

clips.text: The named sources, so you can check me: Glasheen and McMahon’s basilisk model, 1996, in Nature; Hsieh and Lauder’s three-dimensional forces, 2004, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences; Minetti and colleagues’ reduced-gravity running, 2012, in PLoS ONE.
clips.image: A science notebook and three research journals stacked on a desk, a pen resting across the pages, rain on the window behind, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: rule 24: named sources in VO.

clips.text: You step off the kerb — and your shoe stays dry. Next time you step in a puddle without thinking, you will not notice the cold. Now you know what that dry shoe would cost.
clips.image: a young man with brown hair in a blue hoodie walking away from a puddle into the rainy city, his shadow long on the wet asphalt, storm-grey city rain, wet asphalt, slate grey, rain silver, neon reflections in puddles, cinematic wide shot, no text
clips.note: closing line; logical loop back to the opening hook.

clips.text: The water was never a floor — it was a race, won with every step. Goodnight. And if you see a lizard sprint across a river — remember, it is not walking. It is outrunning its own sinking, one slap at a time.
clips.image: A basilisk lizard sprinting across a river at dawn, spray flying from its feet, mist over the water, storm-grey palette, slate grey, rain silver, photorealistic, no text
clips.note: closing echo of the title.
